newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jewish body pressures Swiss over minister's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Jewish body pressures Swiss over minister's remarks.

text.p: The World Jewish Congress (WJC) stepped up pressure on Switzerland on Tuesday by demanding the government criticise the economics minister if it wanted to avoid a boycott of Swiss banks.

WJC Executive Director Elan Steinberg told Switzerland's Tages-Anzeiger newspaper his organisation expected the Swiss cabinet to chastise Jean-Pascal Delamuraz for labelling calls for a Swiss Holocaust compensation fund "blackmail".

"We expect not just one or two cabinet members but the entire Swiss government to distance itself clearly from this comment by their colleague. We await the answer with bated breath," Steinberg said in an interview.

"If it does not come to a formal denial, Jewish restitution organisations...will very well take this into consideration when they discuss in early February officially calling for a boycott of Swiss banks," he added.
A government statement is expected later on Tuesday, officials said.

Swiss banks on Monday expressed dismay over the boycott threats -- first raised in December -- which are weighing on bank stock prices by raising the prospect of damage to their international business.

In some of the strongest language used so far by Berne politicians, Delamuraz last month brushed off demands by the WJC and a U.S. senator for quick compensation for Holocaust survivors and heirs who say Swiss banks have denied them money left there as a safe haven from Nazi looting.

He rejected creation of a $250 million fund he said was proposed to special ambassador Thomas Borer, who met critics from the WJC and U.S. Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato in December.

"This is nothing less than extortion and blackmail. This fund would make it much more difficult to establish the truth," Delamuraz said in a newspaper interview. "Such a fund would be considered an admission of guilt."

Delamuraz repeated Berne's stance that any compensation measures should wait for the findings of a nine-member historical panel appointed by the cabinet in December to investigate the Swiss financial role in World War Two.

Delamuraz, who was ending his one-year term as president at the time he made his comments, has since said he regretted if his remark caused offence, but reiterated the time was not yet ripe for such a fund.
